evidence: deepseek-v4-flash: "DFS to count rented nodes in subtree"
Both implementations accumulate only edge weights in the minimal subtree and assign no cost to intermediate unrented racks.
affordance_in_statement: Data can be routed through racks that the customer has not rented; these unrented racks function as free relay switches, meaning you only pay the activation expenses of the links themselves.
removal_suggestion: Make activating an unrented relay rack incur an additional stated activation expense, so the objective includes both selected-link costs and relay-rack costs rather than only summing the edges in the terminal subtree.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Counts rented terminals in rooted subtrees and adds the weight of every edge whose subtree contains a rented rack.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: The infrastructure has exactly one route between every pair, and unrented racks are free relay switches.

survivor_shortcuts.shortcut: Builds a parent/order traversal and uses parent-edge weights to compute the required terminal subtree.
survivor_shortcuts.affordance: You only pay activation expenses of the links themselves; intermediate unrented racks carry no cost.

common_affordance: Unrented racks used as relays are free, so the answer is obtained solely by summing the costs of the links in the minimal subtree spanning the rented racks.

defeated_student_causes.why_failed: The shown DSU/Kruskal-style approach treats connectivity as component merging and does not correctly force every edge on the unique path between rented racks, especially edges whose endpoints are both unrented relay racks.
The shown solution relies on recursive tree traversal; a valid 200000-vertex path can exceed practical Python recursion/stack limits despite raising the configured recursion limit.

recommended_edit: Replace the sentence saying that unrented racks are free relay switches with a rule that every unrented rack used on an active route also has an activation expense, and require that expense to be included in the minimum.
